title: Reporting and Editing
summary: Reporting is the collection or gathering of facts about current events or background material for a news story or feature, through interviews, investigation and observation. Reporters get assignments (general or special) from editors and write stories called copies. A reporter should write with clarity, objectivity and accuracy. Editing is preparing a news report for publication or broadcast: reading, correcting, modifying, value-adding, polishing and condensing. An editor needs creative skills, command of language and correct judgement of importance. Sanjay, who narrated the Mahabharata war to Dhritarashtra, is called the first war correspondent.

Listening (overheard conversations give clues), covering events, press conferences (leaders, ministers, business houses launching products), reports and statements (commissions, press releases), Parliament and Assemblies (questions, debates, budgets), police sources (crime, accidents), interviews (reactions of people), and also government and non-government sources, courts, airports, railway stations, educational institutions and hospitals.

Hard news (general, breaking, needs immediate publication); soft news (light, not urgent, interesting); features (detailed in-depth stories carried in the magazine section); profiles of newsmakers; human interest stories (plight of individuals or families); backgrounders (history or precedent of an event).

Finding the lead: the lead is the opening sentence and the most important part of a story; it can be hard (serious stories) or soft (human interest and features). Finding the angle: the most vital part of the story, chosen from the facts, depending on the paper and readers (for the union budget, the farmers' debt relief package). Body of the story: the fleshy part with facts and figures, written in the inverted pyramid style, with the most important facts in the opening paragraphs and the least important at the end, so that cutting the end does not affect the impact.
## Qualities of a good news story and reporter

A good story has clarity ('when in doubt, leave it out'), focus, objectivity (balanced, both sides) and credibility (cross-check facts). Breaking news is a report of a sudden development of utmost importance; exclusives or scoops are reports covered by only one reporter. A good reporter has news sense, clarity, objectivity, accuracy, alertness, inquisitiveness, time consciousness, patience, imagination, integrity, fearlessness, tactfulness, mobility and a reading habit. Investigative reporting is in-depth reporting of a scandal or controversy (Bofors, security scam, urea import scam), sometimes a sting operation (Tehelka); interpretative reporting is analysis of developments, mostly by senior journalists on political developments.

The Chief Editor heads all departments and supervises overall; then managing editors and assistant/deputy managing editors; news editors in charge of the news desks; chief sub-editors (desk chiefs); sub-editors; and section editors (sports, feature, picture, business, city or metro editors). Editing a copy: the sub-editor corrects language, spelling, grammar and facts, adds value with background material from the library, writes the heading (sharp, crisp, suggestive, fitting the column and mood, never a full sentence), adds photographs or graphs, condenses the story to fit the space and suggests a byline (a reporter's name credit for an exclusive story; stories of news agencies like PTI and UNI normally carry none). Tools of a sub-editor: a dictionary and reference books, the library and the Internet.

Most newspaper offices have become paperless: filing, editing, photo editing and page setting are done on computers; pages set go directly to press. Page making or layout is preparing the page of the newspaper (earlier on dummy pages, now on the computer screen); every newspaper has about eight columns per page. A photo's caption (catchword) is written by the sub-editor; picture editors select pictures but the news editor decides the number per page. Photo agencies supply pictures from other countries.

Press freedom is the right to publish news without restriction, but one should not publish anything misleading, inaccurate, defamatory, vulgar or obscene, intrude on privacy or harm national interest. The Press and Registration of Books Act 1867 is the oldest press law: every newspaper must print the printer's and publisher's name and the place of printing. A defamed person can file a defamation case; the editor, printer or publisher may be punished individually or jointly.

vsa: What is meant by interpretative reporting?
Reporting that analyses news developments, usually done by senior journalists, mostly on political developments.
What is meant by 'lead' of a news story?
The opening sentence, the most important part, which attracts the reader's attention.
An exclusive news report covered by only one reporter, considered a great achievement.
What is meant by investigative reporting?
In-depth reporting of a scandal or controversy in all its details, sometimes through a sting operation.
Reporting is gathering facts for a news story; editing is correcting, polishing, condensing and preparing it for publication.
sa: Briefly discuss any three basic facts about reporting with examples.

Finding the lead (opening sentence, e.g. 'PM dies in plane crash'); finding the angle (the most vital part, e.g. farmers' debt relief in the budget); body of the story in inverted pyramid style with important facts first.
Which types of news should be refrained from reporting under the ethics of reporting?
Misleading, inaccurate, defamatory, vulgar or obscene news, anything intruding on privacy, and news that harms national interest.
Explain the job of a sub-editor in editing a copy.
Correct language and facts, add background, write a crisp heading, add photographs or graphs, condense to fit space and suggest a byline.
List the qualities of a good news story.
Clarity, focus, objectivity and credibility with cross-checked facts.
la: What is meant by the 'inverted pyramid' method of writing? Explain in detail.

The most important facts come in the opening paragraphs; importance narrows down to the end; the least important details come last and can be cut without harming the story; it keeps the reader's interest and suits the lead.
Describe the sources from which reporters get news.
Listening, covering events, press conferences, reports and statements, Parliament and Assemblies, police sources and interviews.
